seo.title: Game Score in Hockey and How the Formula Works
seo.description: Game score in hockey rolls a player's box score and on-ice results into one number per game. The formula, the benchmarks, and the Red Wings' live leaders.

hero.definition: Game score is a single-game rating that rolls goals, assists, shots, blocks, penalties, faceoffs and on-ice shot and goal results into one number. Dom Luszczyszyn built game score in hockey form in 2016, weighting each piece so a season's total lands close to a player's points. This site averages MoneyPuck's and HockeyStatCards' versions.
hero.dek: Points tell you who scored. Game score asks what else happened while a player was out there, from the shots he took to the penalties he drew to whether his team won the shot battle, and it puts a number on every night of a season.

origin: Game score started in baseball and went through basketball on the way to hockey. Bill James created the baseball version and John Hollinger built the basketball one, and Dom Luszczyszyn credited both when he introduced hockey's at Hockey-Graphs on July 13, 2016, under the title "Measuring Single Game Productivity."

His method was deliberately simple. Each stat was weighted by how often it shows up relative to goals, then the weights were scaled down by 75% so a player's game score would roughly equal his points. Corsi, blocked shots and faceoffs were worth so little already that they weren't scaled any further. Goalies got their own formula, built on goals allowed and saves. The top of the scale is steep. The original piece listed the only games since 2007-08 that rated above 5, and Sam Gagner's eight-point night in 2012 was worth 7.1.

The formula has moved on since. Luszczyszyn added expected goals in 2019, the version NHL.com later described as using "advanced measures of shot quality for and against," and he built his player-value model at The Athletic, Game Score Value Added (GSVA), on the same idea. MoneyPuck's data dictionary carries a gameScore column "as designed by @domluszczyszyn," and HockeyStatCards publishes a game score for every game in a player's log, with links back to both the 2016 article and the 2019 model.

intro: The original skater formula is a weighted sum of 13 counts, positive for the things that help and negative for the things that hurt. Goals carry the most weight and faceoffs the least. These are the inputs:
inputs: Goals, primary assists and secondary assists
On-ice shot attempts for and against at five-on-five
On-ice goals for and against at five-on-five

formulas.label: Season
formulas.expr: season game score = the sum of every game's score

calculation.example: Here's a worked example with invented round numbers. A forward scores once, adds a secondary assist, puts four shots on goal, blocks one, takes a penalty and wins six of ten draws. At five-on-five he's on the ice for a dozen shot attempts for and eight against, and one goal each way (his own included). Run that through the weights and you get 1.72, a good night just short of the 2.0 line this site's game logs highlight. The goal and the assist account for more than three-quarters of it.
after: MoneyPuck applies the box-score terms to all situations and the on-ice terms to five-on-five. Rebuild its season figures for last season from its own columns that way and the formula above lands within 0.01 for 923 of the league's 940 skaters. HockeyStatCards points readers to the 2019 model and shows expected-goal columns beside each game's score, and its numbers don't match MoneyPuck's game for game. This site averages the two (a game only gets a score once both have posted it).

meaning: Game score measures single-game productivity, priced in points.

It's built to land near a player's point total over a season, so Alex DeBrincat's 87.4 in MoneyPuck's file for last season sits right beside his 85 points, even though the shots, blocks and on-ice terms pull some players well above or below their point totals. Per game, the median forward who played 60 games scored 0.53 and the top 10% cleared 1.02. Defensemen sat about a third lower, because the formula pays mostly for points. Nathan MacKinnon led everyone at 1.86 a game, ahead of Nikita Kucherov and Connor McDavid.

DeBrincat was Detroit's best at 1.07, 32nd of the 488 skaters who played 60 games, and Dylan Larkin, Moritz Seider and Lucas Raymond were bunched just under 0.90. If you're scanning a game log, that's the context for a single night's number. Detroit's regulars averaged between zero and a little over one a game, so a 2.0 is a night well above anyone's usual.

Does it repeat? It holds up about as well as points do. For forwards who played 60 games in each of the last two seasons, per-game game score correlated with the next season's at 0.86, against 0.88 for points per game. Luszczyszyn called it fairly repeatable in 2016, and the numbers back him.

uses.title: Grading one night
uses.html: That's the job it was built for. What counts as a good night? Every Red Wings player page here logs a game score for each game, with 2.0 marking a strong one and anything below zero a poor one, plus a ten-game rolling average so you can see a hot or cold stretch forming before the season totals do. The chart colors each bar by sign, so a run of poor nights stands out.

uses.title: Ranking players early in a season
uses.html: This site's W-Value needs Evolving-Hockey's numbers, which aren't there at the start of a season. Until they are, each player page ranks him on cumulative game score among every NHL skater who's played, on the same 0 to 100 scale, and labels it as a stand-in. It's a rough proxy for value, built from the box score, and it gives way to the W-Value once that can be computed.

uses.title: Crediting the work behind the points
uses.html: Seider and Raymond finished last season with almost the same game score on very different point totals, 60 and 76. Seider's 180 blocked shots were worth 9.0 on their own, and Detroit's five-on-five shot attempts ran 176 ahead of opponents' with him on the ice, worth 8.8 more. Ben Chiarot went the other way. His 15 points became a 9.3 game score, dragged down by a five-on-five attempt margin of minus-218.

limits.title: The weights are a judgment call
limits.html: Luszczyszyn set each weight by how often that stat turns into goals and then rounded it, so nothing in the formula was fit to winning, and a shot on goal is worth 0.075 because of how often shots become goals.

limits.title: It's mostly points
limits.html: Goals and assists made up 68% of the game score earned by the league's forwards who played 60 games last season. A defenseman who doesn't produce points can't climb far, however well you think he defends.

limits.title: Shot volume counts twice
limits.html: Every shot on goal earns its own 0.075, and the same shot feeds the on-ice Corsi term (a second, smaller credit). DeBrincat's 287 shots on goal were worth 21.5 of his 87.4, a quarter of his season total.

limits.title: The versions disagree
limits.html: MoneyPuck's number reproduces the 2016 formula, while HockeyStatCards points to the 2019 model with expected goals in it, so the same game can grade as a good night on one site and an ordinary one on the other. Averaging the two smooths that out without settling which is right.

method: League figures are Wes & Woodward's calculations from MoneyPuck's 2025-26 regular-season skater file (downloaded October 9, 2026) and its 2024-25 file (downloaded October 9, 2026, saved as raw/mp_skaters_2024_repeatability.csv). Per-game game score is MoneyPuck's season gameScore ÷ games played, all situations, among skaters with 60+ games; the formula check rebuilds gameScore from the same file's all-situations box-score columns and five-on-five on-ice columns; term contributions use the 2016 weights; repeatability is the Pearson correlation of per-game game score (and points per game) between seasons for the 260 forwards with 60+ games in both. The site's per-game blend and the 2.0 highlight line come from pipeline/build_player.py and the player page.
